#2718. Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off

As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.

On platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.

Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.

On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.

The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.

The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.

"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.

The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.

In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

#2717. Colts sign Shane Buechele and Wanya Morris in flurry of roster moves, place Caden Curry on IR

The Indianapolis Colts made a series of roster moves Tuesday, signing quarterback Shane Buechele from the Buffalo Bills' practice squad, promoting defensive end Carl Lawson to the 53-man roster and placing rookie defensive end Caden Curry on injured reserve. The organization also waived offensive tackle Charlie Heck while adding tight end Sean McKeon and defensive end Cam Sample to the practice squad, according to the team's official announcement.

Indianapolis wasn't finished there, as ESPN's Adam Schefter also reported that the Colts are signing offensive tackle Wanya Morris from the Dallas Cowboys' practice squad to their active roster, providing additional help to an offensive line that has been severely affected by injuries throughout the season.

The addition of Buechele comes just days after Indianapolis released Daniel Jones and announced that Anthony Richardson would return as the starting quarterback for the remainder of the 2026 season. With Richardson now receiving another opportunity to prove himself and Riley Leonard also on the roster, Buechele provides additional depth and experience in a quarterback room that has undergone considerable changes.

Buechele entered the NFL as an undrafted free agent with the Kansas City Chiefs in 2021 after playing collegiately at Texas and SMU. He spent several seasons developing behind Patrick Mahomes before joining Buffalo in 2023, where he spent time on both the active roster and practice squad. His only regular-season appearance came with Kansas City in 2025, when he completed seven of 14 passes for 88 yards. While he is unlikely to challenge Richardson for the starting job, his familiarity with NFL systems gives Indianapolis another option as it navigates the final six games of the season.

Morris, meanwhile, represents an interesting addition given the current state of the Colts' offensive line. The 26-year-old was selected in the third round of the 2023 NFL Draft by Kansas City and appeared in 43 games, making 16 starts during his three seasons with the Chiefs. He was traded to Atlanta during the offseason before being released in August, eventually joining Dallas' practice squad.

Indianapolis has been forced to make significant adjustments at offensive tackle following injuries to Bernhard Raimann and Jalen Travis. With Raimann dealing with a concussion and Travis sidelined by a knee injury, the Colts started Luke Tenuta at left tackle and moved Matt Goncalves to right tackle against Houston. Morris provides another experienced option at a position where the team has struggled to maintain continuity, while Heck's departure ends a brief stint in Indianapolis after signing with the organization on October 29.

On the defensive side, the promotion of Lawson comes at the expense of losing another promising young contributor.

Curry, a sixth-round selection in the 2026 NFL Draft, has appeared in all 11 games this season, recording 14 tackles, one sack, two fumble recoveries and 12 special teams stops. The former Ohio State defensive end has provided useful depth along the defensive line while establishing himself as a dependable contributor on special teams. His placement on injured reserve means he will be required to miss at least four games, a disappointing development for a rookie who had begun carving out a role within the organization.

Lawson should help compensate for that absence, providing Indianapolis with an experienced pass rusher who has recorded 32 sacks across his NFL career. The former Cincinnati Bengals fourth-round pick joined the Colts' practice squad in October and was previously elevated for the team's matchup against Jacksonville, recording one tackle. Although he is no longer the player who consistently generated pressure earlier in his career, he offers additional experience to a defensive front that has already undergone considerable changes following DeForest Buckner's departure.

The Colts also added two familiar NFL veterans to their practice squad in McKeon and Sample.

McKeon returns to Indianapolis after previously spending time with the organization during the 2024 and 2025 seasons, as well as participating in this year's offseason program and training camp. His addition provides additional tight end depth following Mo Alie-Cox's placement on injured reserve earlier this month.

Sample, meanwhile, was originally selected by Cincinnati in the fourth round of the 2021 NFL Draft and has appeared in 61 career games, recording seven sacks. The veteran defensive end has spent time with the Bengals, 49ers and Falcons, and could provide another option for Indianapolis should additional injuries occur along the defensive line.

With the Colts sitting at 3-8 and preparing to face the New York Giants on Sunday, the latest moves reflect an organization attempting to manage mounting injuries while continuing to evaluate its roster for the future. Richardson's return has already brought significant changes to the offense, and the additions of Buechele and Morris provide some much-needed depth at two important positions.

While none of these transactions is likely to dramatically change the team's outlook over the final six games, they should help Indianapolis navigate the remainder of an increasingly difficult season while giving several players an opportunity to demonstrate whether they deserve a role moving forward.

#2716. The Nasdaq is in freefall. Here's one stock to look at

I asked Claude after Friday's close what I should do about the tanking stock market. Its advice was surprisingly useful: avoid panic selling and look for opportunities. A 40 VIX, which it touched Friday, might provide those opportunities. Specifically, a higher VIX (higher options premiums) signals fear, but it also creates an opportunity to sell elevated premium in some premium stocks, like Amazon.

Amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. Trailing 12-month operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion. However, infrastructure investment accelerated, resulting in more than $42 billion in negative cash flow. The competing forces of accelerating growth and the cost of supplying it could keep the stock in its range over the next four weeks. Its shares are only off 14% from its recent highs, comparatively better than the Nasdaq Composite's near 19% decline.

AWS demand supports the lower end of the range. The backlog gives Amazon a basis for adding capacity even as investors scrutinize the cash cost. Cash spending could temper an upside rerating.

The next leg higher may require evidence that new capacity can earn attractive returns at this scale, and that evidence may be in short supply over the next couple of months.

Sell the Dec. 18, 2026 AMZN 235/285 strangle for an indicative $5.90 credit per share.

Max reward — $590 per strangle if AMZN finishes between $235 and $285 at expiration, before fees.

Breakevens at expiration — $229.10 and $290.90.

Max risk — Unlimited on the uncovered call, but one should think of the trade as risking getting short at a net price above $290, a nearly 13% premium to today's closing price. The downside loss would reach $22,910 per strangle if AMZN fell to zero. The credit is roughly 2.3% of a $260 reference share price over four weeks, or nearly 30% on a simple annualized basis. That comparison uses the share price as its denominator. Actual return on capital depends on margin and the cost to close or settle the trade.

Buying in bear markets, as the Nasdaq just touched, is never easy. But those opportunities don't present themselves too often. What are you going to do with it?

#2715. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander lost a trash-talk battle to a Pacers bench warmer

Shai Gilgeous-Alexander is one of 14 players in NBA history to win back-to-back MVPs. Jalen Slawson doesn't even have a real roster spot on the Indiana Pacers, instead playing on a "two-way" deal designed to shuffle him between the G League and the big leagues. On Monday night, two unlikely adversaries produced some of the best trash talk of the NBA season, and somehow Slawson came out on top.

The Pacers beat the Thunder, 125-120, in a 2025 NBA Finals rematch for two teams missing some of their best players. Indiana continues to be without Tyrese Haliburton as he works his way back from a hamstring injury. OKC is trying to survive long-term injuries to Jalen Williams, Chet Holmgren, and Cason Wallace.

The trash talk started at the end of the second quarter when Slawson had an incredible block on an SGA drive to the rim. When Slawson hit a three over an SGA contest two possessions later, he immediately started taunting the two-time MVP again. Gilgeous-Alexander would strike back before the end of the half by hitting a three over Slawson and immediately doing the same celebration he had just done to him. Watch the sequence here:

Slawson and the Pacers would get the last laugh even though he didn't score in the fourth quarter. SGA only shot 3-of-8 from the floor in the final period for seven points, and also had two turnovers. SGA finished the night with 38 points on 13-of-30 shooting with seven assists. Slawson had 16 points, 10 rebounds, and four blocks in 20 minutes off the bench.

Slawson was on our list of players who looked too good for Las Vegas Summer League this year. He's a big, athletic forward out of Furman who can get downhill and provide some supplemental rim protection, and he's been making steady progress with his three-point shot over the last couple years in the G League.

With so much attrition on both sides, players are being forced into unnatural roles. For Gilgeous-Alexander, that means putting up the highest usage rate of his career, a ridiculous 37%. For Slawson, that means playing real NBA minutes for the first time in his career. For one night, it produced the most unlikely showdown possible.

#2713. Bucks Reacts Survey: Are your vibes still high?

Welcome to SB Nation Reacts, a survey of fans across the NBA. Throughout the year we ask questions of the most plugged-in Bucks fans and fans across the country.

Back in September, we gauged your enthusiasm for the season ahead, asking if you were more or less excited for this season than last. As it turned out, you were much more excited for this season. Since then, however, there's been a whole lotta losing. But has that been enough to kill your vibes, or, as they have for resident commenter Boom_Shakalaka, have the young Bucks done enough to fill your cup?

As it stands, the Bucks sit 15th in the Eastern Conference with a 2-16 record. In the process, they've earned the not-so-enviable records of worst start to a season in franchise history and second-longest losing streak in franchise history (13 in a row, prior to last night's win against the Toronto Raptors). Unsurprisingly, they also have the second-worst point differential in the entire league (-11.4 PPG), ahead of only the 2-16 and seemingly always-inept Sacramento Kings (-12.5 PPG). Yet, despite Sacramento's lengthy run of failures—only twice in the last 20 years have they had a winning record—the Kings have the better average attendance, attracting an average crowd of 14,345 people this year to the Bucks' 13,296 (which ranks dead last).

On a player level, there's been plenty to gripe about too. Last night aside, Myles Turner has been okay at best and woeful at worst, while Kyle Kuzma continues his Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde play to the ire of fans. Jaime Jaquez Jr. has cooled off considerably after some hot form early, and Ryan Rollins has been a shell of the player he was last season, at least on the offensive end. For all his talent, Kel'el Ware has been similarly underwhelming.

Despite the losing, there's been plenty for Bucks fans to cheer (okay, quietly bump their fists) about. Rookies Brayden Burries and Nate Ament are playing more often and looking even better than we could have hoped for—especially at this early stage of the season. Burries, in particular, has been outstanding, playing every game (including 10 starts) and putting up 11.4 PPG, 5.7 RPG, 2.5 APG, 0.9 SPG and just 1.4 TOV on .455/.313/.741 shooting splits. Beyond the numbers, he's looked every bit the seasoned pro, consistently one of Milwaukee's better rebounders and downhill scorers, and, at times, even looking like the team's best player. Ament, while not as spectacular, has arguably been even more surprising. He's played in 16 games (two starts) and has proven to be a reliable shooter, opportunistic rim finisher, and legitimately good on-ball defender on his way to averages of 7.6 PPG and 3.1 RPG on .453/.349/.750 shooting. Beyond those two, Kasparas Jakučionis has had more than a few moments—including a Brew Hoop MVB and Defensive Belt double—while Tyler Herro has largely been good and, on occasion, unbelievable. Others have had moments too.

Recently, despite the continually fluctuating and at times infuriating rotation, the Bucks have also looked much more cohesive as a whole. They had a very real shot at winning against the Portland Trail Blazers, should have won—or at least gone into overtime—against the Philadelphia 76ers, and did put it all together in an uplifting win over the Raptors in Canada. Sweetening that win was Turner's play. Where he'd looked out of sorts earlier in the season—perhaps most noticeably against the same Raptors team—he was decisive in this one: engaged on both ends; dynamic as a spacer and finisher inside; and a defensive presence, both as a rim protector and rebounder. That this performance came against the very team that could potentially seek Turner's services in exchange for draft capital makes it even sweeter. Keep it coming, big fella!

Taking all of this into consideration—the "little wins" highs and the lower-than-Lil-Jon-can-make-you-get lows—just how much are you enjoying this season?

#2712. Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns

Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta said. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

Mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the company to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

"Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

Mehta ranks No. 876 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 8.1%. See Devon Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. ET's cash distribution for Q3 2026 was 34.25 cents per common unit, up more than 3% year-over-year. At an annualized distribution of $1.37 per share, Energy Transfer yields more than 7%.

TD Cowen analyst Jason Gabelman reiterated a buy rating on Energy Transfer with a price target of $25. The company delivered better-than-expected Q3 results and announced the 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) South Mississippi Pipeline, a 215-mile, 36-inch natural gas line linking the Perryville Hub to the Florida Gas Transmission (FGT) network, Gabelman said. The project is supported by 20-year firm transportation agreements and is expected to enter service in 2030. ET expects to ultimately own 51% of the $1.6 billion project.

The 5-star analyst said that Energy Transfer lowered its 2026 capital spending outlook to $5.5 billion (midpoint of the guidance range) from $5.75 billion due to project timing. Energy Transfer expects capex to rise to $7 billion in 2027, while Gabelman projects $5 billion in both 2028 and 2029, based on disclosed projects.

Gabelman also highlighted management's commentary about optimization initiatives contributing an incremental $800 million to 2026 earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization, a larger benefit than in recent years. "A return to less commodity volatility should the [Middle East] war end could bring some relative downside, though this is offset by continued strong growth prospects," he said.

Gabelman ranks No. 397 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 64% of the time, delivering an average return of 15.4%. See Energy Transfer KPIs on TipRanks.

Oil and gas exploration and production company ConocoPhillips (COP) delivered better-than-expected Q3 performance. The company announced an 11% hike in its quarterly dividend to 93 cents per share, effective with the Q4 dividend payable on December 1. Based on the dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, COP yields about 2.6%.

Following the Q3 results, Wells Fargo analyst Sam Margolin repeated a buy rating on ConocoPhillips, citing strong potential for further dividend increases. Margolin also trimmed his price target to $185 from $189 to reflect timing effects and the WAHA forward curve, though he said that COP could still re-rate as its natural portfolio lifecycle provides stronger protection against inflationary pressures than peers. The Waha forward curve tracks future natural gas prices based on the West Texas Waha hub.

Margolin, another 5-star analyst, highlighted that ConocoPhillips' Q3 2026 adjusted earnings per share of $3.27 was well above Wells Fargo and the Street's estimates of $3.04 and $3.05, respectively. Earnings were driven by solid price realizations, partially offset by higher depletion, depreciation and amortization and purchased commodities.

Margolin also noted COP's dividend increase and said the accelerated buyback enabled by current commodity prices could further support long-term dividend growth. He sees the possibility of ConocoPhillips' dividend growth rate exceeding its current 6% cost of equity into the end of the decade. Margolin expects COP to sustain an 8% dividend compound annual growth rate through 2029 while repurchasing $6.4 billion of stock annually, and reducing net debt-to-capital to less than 9% by the end of 2028 based on the assumption of an average Brent crude oil price of $75 a barrel.

"The message on the 3Q call was similar to that of 2Q, reiterating the moderation in reinvestment rate and commitment to dividend growth through the Willow start-up and after," Margolin said.

#2711. Mavericks vs. Nuggets predictions: Odds, recent stats, trends and best bets for November 24

The Dallas Mavericks (10-7) and the Denver Nuggets (10-5) each bring a three-game winning streak into tonight's matchup at Ball Arena. Dallas enters at 10-7 overall and 3-5 on the road, while Denver is 10-5 overall and 4-3 at home. The Nuggets continue to rely on their offense. They average 117.0 points per game on 49 percent shooting, compared with 112.4 points for the Mavericks. Dallas earned their third straight win Sunday, surviving a remarkable late rally to beat the Utah Jazz 116-114. Dallas used a 20-5 third quarter run to build an 18-point advantage and still led 114-98 with 2:14 remaining, only for Utah to score 16 unanswered points and tie the game with 4.7 seconds left. Cooper Flagg answered by making two decisive free throws with 3.7 seconds remaining, completing a 28-point performance, before Utah missed a three-pointer at the buzzer. Kyrie Irving scored all 16 of his points in the first half, while Dallas converted Utah's 23 turnovers into 32 points. Flagg is averaging 24.3 points, 6.3 rebounds and 6.4 assists, with P.J. Washington adding 14.0 points and a team-high 6.7 rebounds per game.

#2708. The biggest money-making energy trade looks over. What to buy instead

Is one of the greatest money-making trades of the last few years coming to an end?

No, I'm not talking about Nvidia or any of the data center- or AI-related power companies (although they have been crushed lately too… more on that on CNBC TV. Tune in!).

I'm talking about whether the epic boom in refinery-related stocks is unwinding. Over the last year, the jump in some of these companies has been nothing short of remarkable.

That jump is largely due to massive increases in margins, earnings, and cash flow. Those have occurred because of a big jump in what is called a crack spread. That is the difference between the price of oil and the finished price of refined products such as diesel and jet fuel. For most of this year, spreads have been soaring as disruptions and attacks on facilities and shipping in the Arabian Gulf, Hormuz, and deep inside Russia have played havoc with the market. In the last week or so, however, something big has changed: many of those spreads have started to tighten.

This seismic drop in spreads is causing a selloff in the aforementioned refinery companies.

If spreads continue to fall, these stocks may well keep selling off from recent highs. The upshot for investors may be that, as the shares come down, analysts see more upside. The median price target for Phillips 66 (PSX) now indicates a 20% gain from here, while smaller-cap Par Pacific (PARR) is double that.

Here are a few other key points to focus on heading into the Thanksgiving-shortened week.

I like to keep politics as much at arm's length as possible — we all know that energy and politics (sadly) often go hand in hand. Energy policies coming from Washington, D.C., can drive — or destroy — investment dollars. With all the big shifts in the White House over the last 10 years (four years of Trump, four years of Biden, and now 2 years into Trump #2), energy policies can blow through Washington faster than a summer squall hits a wind turbine. But because federal policies can mean so much for specific companies, sectors, and investments, it's important to follow the news flow.

That said, I'd like to take a moment to introduce you to the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, known as BAAJA (and pronounced like the state in Mexico). Like much legislation, BAAJA is an obscure but important bill working its way through the American Congress. BAAJA does a lot of things, but what Power Insider readers care about is its focus on energy permitting reform. In a nutshell, BAAJA would help speed up the building of new electricity infrastructure. Again, that's an overly simplistic view of a big bill, but it needs to be on your radar. The utility trade group Edison Electric Institute came out in favor of the legislation this month after the industry received some 11th-hour changes. See more about it in our recent interview with EEI President Drew Maloney here.

The bill passed the U.S. Senate in a vote late Thursday night. Now it moves to the House. Support for its final passage is also coming from the big LNG trade group, whose executive director said he "applauds the Senate for its bipartisan effort to pass meaningful, bipartisan, and durable permitting reforms aimed at delivering greater predictability, consistency, and certainty in the permitting, production, and export process for U.S. LNG. This legislation moves us closer to untangling red tape and eliminating overlapping agency reviews that can keep U.S. energy projects delayed for years."

The Natural Gas Supply Association also chimed in, saying it urges Congress to see the bill as "a resource-agnostic and balanced reform agenda for boosting American energy security. It keeps strong environmental reviews in place, but it draws a firm line against the endless procedural delays that tie critical energy projects in knots for a decade."

In my view, passing BAAJA is an important test of Congress's appetite for helping the energy and electrical power industry, lowering costs, and speeding time to market. The old adage was correct: time is money. Literally. If BAAJA moves on through the House, we could see an upside move in some utility stocks and any company related to energy infrastructure.

Speaking of politics, the news is getting lost in the massive Anthropic (ANT) IPO, but the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) — whose importance I wrote about in the last edition — just decided to resume permitting for data centers. The Texas Tribune did a nice write-up on it, and you can read it here.

It's tough to say, but it's true. The two are inextricably linked by policies created at both the federal and state levels. As I wrote in the last edition, some federally elected officials may have less impact on state-level issues — like the data center buildout — but they certainly have power over national laws. While many of you are enthralled, disgusted, or confused by sordid tales of Nvidia and Jensen-gate, keep one eye open on what happens in Washington, D.C.

Have a great week, and have a wonderful Thanksgiving, everyone.

Perhaps the big investor story — which is, like most things lately, related to Jensen-gate and Nvidia—is the sizable selloff in many AI, neocloud, and data center power-related stocks.

Painful for current shareholders, but big drops can also bring big opportunities. Wall Street believes that's the case, at least right now. Look at some of the potential upside based on the stocks' prices versus their price targets.

We spoke with the CEO of Applied Digital (APLD) about all of this on CNBC last week, and you can watch it here. He highlighted how the market may be getting these stock stories wrong because, at least with his company, he has long-term contracts with solid-credit companies. In that way, Applied Digital is more like a landlord than a "pure-play" AI company.

My take → While I'm not going to recommend a specific stock, I would add that it is critical for investors to understand the differences between these companies. While they may have some things in common, they are also different, with different business models, customers, leases, and sources of revenue.

Speaking of recommendations… here are two ideas for you:

A recent decline presents a nice opportunity in SOLV Energy (MWH). UBS analyst Jon Windham upgrades SOLV to buy from neutral, believing the market is "underappreciating several key tailwinds for SOLV given uncertainty around data center demand and higher interest rates." UBS highlights how the stock has fallen lately despite making two deals and beating and raising recent guidance. UBS says now is an "attractive entry point" for SOLV. (Side note: MWH is a great stock ticker.)

While markets overall fall, BMO remains bullish on Bloom Energy (BE). After speaking with the company, the analyst is upgrading Bloom to outperform, saying he remains "increasingly confident of BE's commercial traction" and that he still has conviction even with the recent drop in shares. While analyst Ameet Thakkar did cut his target to $230 from $260, that's still 50% upside from the current price. Bloom shares have tumbled 45% since October 1.

I was recently asked for my opinion on the price of oil. Here's my take. The market clearly wants to push oil contract prices lower and has for a few months. But, as I've said and reported for a while, don't confuse the futures (paper) price with the actual price. Yes, shipping rates and insurance rates have come down from recent highs — and there is a good amount of oil now flowing through Hormuz — but the cost of a physical barrel of crude is still well above the futures contract. If we get real, longer-lasting peace around Iran, oil prices will fall. There is plenty of oil in the world. That said, if bombs and missiles start firing again, oil prices will firm. I know that's a non-answer answer, but the oil market is truly headline-driven right now. My late good friend Boone Pickens (later in life, he didn't like being called by the "T" in his first name) used to avoid giving a set price target and instead give a directional quote, so I'll do the same: the odds of oil being lower in two months than it is today are 75%.

Last week, I had a one-on-one with Vimal Kapur, chair and CEO of Honeywell International (HON), at an RBC conference in New York City. While the conversation wasn't filmed, I can tell you that Kapur offered investors reassurance that his order book is doing very, very well. This is important because Honeywell is huge in the things that make other things work. Its sensors go into a ton of energy facilities, from refineries to LNG facilities. Honeywell is a leading indicator of spending and buildouts, so if it keeps getting orders, it's a good sign for macro energy.

Bottom line: Watch Honeywell stock as a potential "tell."

This week's Inside Line interview takes a different approach. We hit our friend Craig Johnson up for actionable insights into energy and stocks. Craig is managing director and chief market technician at Piper Sandler. He recently appeared on Power Lunch to talk about markets and stocks. He mentioned being bullish on energy, so we wanted to dig in just a little bit more.

This week, we had the pleasure of chatting with Balaji Krishnamurthy, president of Chevron Australia. We spoke at length about natural gas, the impact of disruptions, and long-term demand from Chevron customers in the Asia-Pacific region.

This is a bit of a local RBI for the New York City area, but one I felt was important to highlight. New York's electric grid operator just came out with a massive warning for everyone in our region: in just a couple of years, there may not be enough electricity supply to power our needs. A new report shows a deficit in seven years, with a nearly 2 GW power hole in a decade. That's a number of big power plants' worth of energy. Get your solar panels on and buy that backup generator! I'll call this one random, but scary.

Catch up with more on energy including interviews and video content from CNBC and Power Insider.

#2707. Nvidia surge: What investors should do with the stock and the AI trade now

Nvidia shares gapped higher at the open by more than 30%, on pace for its biggest one-day gain in 23 years on Monday, following the news just before the bell that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is going to be reinstated.

Investors and traders said that while this reflex rally may have more to run, cautiousness is warranted on Nvidia and the AI trade because of the overhang of investigations into the alleged Chinese espionage involving the company and others, as well as the possibility for data center moratoriums as Democrats take control of Congress and key governor posts in January.

"Am I as bullish on Nvidia now as I was on Friday? Of course not, you can't be," said Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, which counted Nvidia as its largest position as he bought on the dip over the last few weeks. "I'm trimming back."

"All the same issues that were here before Jensen resigned are still here," he added.

The day before Huang resigned on Nov. 12 as CEO, Nvidia closed at $173.73. It's intraday high on Monday was $171.50, up from its recent low around $125 as it was selling off in the wake controversies. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF closed at $506.96 the day before his resignation. It reached a high of $469.35 before losing steam as trading wore on Monday.

Mike Khouw, YieldMax strategist at Tidal Financial Group, told CNBC on Monday that there were "sighs of relief," "applause" and even "cheering" among investors at the news of Huang's potential reinstatement. But he also said there are still considerable risks facing the AI trade.

Jensen Huang was not the only problem at Nvidia, he said, and there are still many vulnerabilities in the overall AI trade, which should give investors pause. Credit-sensitive companies are still at risk of faltering, Khouw added.

The national security implications of the scandal that has rocked Nvidia and the global AI trade more broadly aren't going away any time soon even as the Trump administration assured the Nvidia board there were none. Investors on Wall Street are expressing strategic concerns about ways to play the tech space just as lawmakers in Washington are demanding answers.

Democrats are demanding answers on what exactly happened with Nvidia and the Chinese government.

"The reckless decision to bring Jensen Huang back as CEO does not change the fact that Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and the company's board still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls," Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said in a Monday statement. "The Trump Administration also needs to explain to Congress what 'input' was given and by which senior officials in the United States government to support his reinstatement."

House Ways and Means ranking member Richard Neal (D-Mass.) stressed the importance of Congressional oversight in determining the best course of action to move forward. The outcome of any Congressional investigations will likely be crucial for Nvidia's long-term viability as an investment opportunity, especially since the company does so much international business.

"This is an export control issue," Neal told CNBC on Monday. "Congress is not subservient to this president or any other president as it relates to trade and tariff policies. This is a trade related issue."

Many of the same Democrats will call for a slowdown in the data center buildout, a strong issue for the public partly responsible for their Blue Wave earlier this month.

"You're going to have to work your way through what these data center moratoriums all mean," said Niles. "Now I think the broader market keeps going but I am not as convinced on the move in the data-center centric names from here."

To be sure, many Wall Street analysts were rushing to upgrade Nvidia's stock on Monday after Huang's reinstatement. Most restored price targets well above $200 with one as high as $270. But many traders think the rebound may fail before getting back to those levels.

Famed short seller Michael Burry, who made a boatload betting against Nvidia with put options as it cratered, told his Substack audience that he thinks the rebound here could be "outsized," especially with low volume in the market overall because of the Thanksgiving holiday this week.

But he too sees the rally eventually losing steam.

"Jensen being back without much more information might even restore NVDA to the high 100s," Burry wrote. "I won't short it on this information I have today until it gets closer to or maybe hurdles $200."

#2706. ESPN hints at potentially massive contract extension for Caleb Williams

Chicago Bears quarterback Caleb Williams could be about to rewrite the contract record books this coming offseason.

At this point, it goes without saying that the third-year signal-caller will get a monster bag as Chicago's franchise quarterback when he becomes eligible for a contract extension this coming spring. ESPN's Courtney Cronin suggested as much in her latest blurb on the Bears and the top extension candidates for each team (aka Williams).

But her projection makes my preseason estimates sound tame.

"Chicago's front office has an incentive to get ahead of a rapidly inflating QB market, which will see the likes of C.J. Stroud and Lamar Jackson come to the table, along with others in Williams' draft class. Though Williams said in September that "money's not a motivating factor for me," his top-10 play on a contending team could lead to him earning around $70 million per year. Signing Williams early would allow the Bears to keep his 2027 cap hit low while prorating a massive signing bonus into future years," she wrote.

Then again, perhaps it shouldn't be surprising.

Right now, Patrick Mahomes boasts the highest average annual value among NFL quarterbacks, earning $63.09 million per year on his reworked contract, followed by Dak Prescott ($60 million) and Josh Allen ($55 million). At least four quarterbacks—Jackson, Stroud, Williams, and Drake Maye—are in line to potentially break those records this offseason as the salary cap continues to climb. (Jayden Daniels is a sneaky candidate as well, though his struggle to stay healthy could hold him back slightly.)

Of the five names listed above, only Jackson is definitively a better player than Williams. Moreover, Williams might be the only one of those players to lead their teams to the playoffs this season, which would be his second trip to the postseason in a row. Throw in his major improvement as a passer, and you have the recipe for a gargantuan payday.

What will be curious, however, is how Williams handles the contract situation in reality.

The young quarterback, who has plenty of endorsements and outside investments, isn't hurting for cash. While he shouldn't take a lowball offer simply for the sake of a hometown discount, it wouldn't be shocking to see him hold back on breaking the bank just enough to make sure the Bears can keep players in town. After all, quarterbacks are important, but they can't win Super Bowls alone.

With the race to $70 million AAV likely to be intense, maybe paying Williams that amount is inevitable for the Bears. But when you have a franchise quarterback, you pay him like one. Fortunately for the Bears, Williams seems like the kind of player who can be worth the price.

#2705. Wolverines in the NFL: TE Marlin Klein catches first career TD

A rookie tight end score his first career touchdown, while a punter made an incredible throw to keep a drive alive on fourth down. Here is this week's Wolverines in the NFL recap.

Wide receiver Nico Collins put Houston ahead for good Thursday night with a 42-yard touchdown catch late in the first quarter. That play in and of itself was worth celebrating, but so was a rookie catching his first career touchdown in the NFL.

Marlin Klein caught the touchdown that finished off Indianapolis. Klein's first NFL touchdown came from 13 yards out in the third quarter and capped Houston's 26-3 win. He caught all four of his targets for 24 yards.

Collins finished with three catches for 58 yards, with his touchdown accounting for the longest gain by either former Wolverine.

Buffalo faced a 4th-and-8 from its own 34 in the first quarter against Miami on Sunday. Buffalo punter Tommy Doman Jr. took the snap and lofted a pass to a wide-open target for 30 yards. A few plays later, Doman was back on the field to hold for the 54-yard field goal his throw helped set up. That put Buffalo ahead 6-0 on its way to a 26-9 win.

Elsewhere, Kenneth Grant started on Miami's defensive line and finished with two tackles. Josh Uche also made a solo tackle.

Dominic Zvada tied Jacksonville with a 53-yard field goal in the first quarter, then hit from a yard farther out with 11 seconds left before halftime. After missing wide left from 32, he connected from 43 in the fourth quarter. Add in two extra points, and Zvada accounted for 11 points in New York's 23-18 win.

With Jon Runyan Jr. starting at left guard, quarterback J.J. McCarthy went 18-of-38 for 173 yards, a touchdown and no interceptions. His eight-yard touchdown pass gave the Giants a 17-6 lead in the second quarter. McCarthy also ran seven times for 33 yards, including a 22-yard gain. Jacksonville cornerback Jourdan Lewis made two tackles.

Colston Loveland caught all three of his targets for 29 yards in Chicago's 21-13 win over New Orleans. His biggest grab came midway through the second quarter, when he hauled in a 15-yard touchdown — and hurdled a guy in the process — to put the Bears ahead 16-0.

Linebacker Devin Bush made eight tackles for Chicago, while Cesar Ruiz started at right guard for the Saints.

Tampa Bay had 4th-and-14 and one more chance to make it a game. With 3:23 left, edge rusher Derrick Moore got a sack on Baker Mayfield a nine-yard loss, giving Detroit the ball at the Bucs' 34. The Lions turned that field position into the touchdown that sealed a 31-21 win. Moore finished with two tackles and half of a sack. Meanwhile, Ben Bredeson started at left guard for Tampa Bay.

Eagles 19, Steelers 16: Joe Milton III started at quarterback for Philadelphia and went 11-of-21 for 141 yards without an interception. He added seven yards on five carries. Pittsburgh wide receiver Roman Wilson caught three passes for 43 yards, including a 33-yard gain in the third quarter.

Cowboys 51, Titans 30: Edge rusher Rashan Gary made two tackles for Dallas, while tight end Luke Schoonmaker caught his only target for six yards.

49ers 35, Vikings 10: Safety Josh Metellus assisted on five tackles for Minnesota in Mexico City. Max Bredeson played 11 offensive snaps at fullback.

Broncos 38, Raiders 24: Kwity Paye started at defensive end for Las Vegas and finished with four tackles.

Panthers 35, Ravens 33: Matt Hibner started at tight end for Baltimore and caught both targets for 12 yards.

Commanders 22, Bengals 20: Defensive backs Daxton Hill and DJ Turner, and defensive tackle Kris Jenkins Jr. combined for 10 total tackles for Cincinnati on Monday Night Football. Washington's Mike Sainristil chipped in three tackles.

#2704. Seahawks sign offensive tackle off Bills’ practice squad

A day after veteran tackle Bobby Hart was signed to the 53-man roster, the Seattle Seahawks have added another offensive lineman to the roster.

The team signed tackle Chase Lundt off the Buffalo Bills' practice squad, The Ringer's Tom Pelissero reported on Tuesday. In a corresponding move, cornerback Avery Smith was waived by the Seahawks.

The 26-year-old Lundt was a sixth-round pick of the Bills in the 2025 NFL Draft, and played two games in a rookie season spent on their active roster. After he was waived during roster cuts ahead of the 2026 season, he was signed to their practice squad where he had remained until Tuesday.

A four-year starter at UConn, Lundt was a collegiate teammate of former Seattle guard Christian Haynes, now of the Miami Dolphins.

Lundt and Hart both joining the roster appear to be insurance for right tackle Abe Lucas, who is dealing with an ankle injury and is a question mark for Week 12 against the San Francisco 49ers.

Smith's departure from the Seahawks comes a day after veteran Trevon Diggs, like Hart, was signed to the active roster off the practice squad. The 22-year-old appeared in six games with Seattle after the team acquired him from the L.A. Chargers for a sixth-round pick ahead of the regular season.

After moving a 2027 day-three selection in order to acquire Smith just a few months ago, the Seahawks will presumably be interested in signing him to their practice squad, should he clear waivers.

#2703. Kalshi daily volume of ‘perps’ trading begins to top its prediction markets

Kalshi is known for its prediction markets across sports, politics and culture.

But now, for the first time, perpetual futures, Kalshi's second financial product, has surpassed the notional trading volume of its event contracts on consecutive days.

On Thursday, perpetual futures — commonly known as "perps" — on Kalshi saw $3.4 billion in notional volume as artificial intelligence laboratory Anthropic stock debuted on public markets while the rest of the market sold off. That exceeded about $3 billion in notional volume for Kalshi's prediction markets on the same day.

Perps are futures-style contracts where there is no expiration and traders do not need to own the underlying asset. Contracts instead continuously track the price of an asset, with funding payments to keep the contract price aligned with that of the market. Funding payments are made periodically between holders of short or long positions.

Perps trading surpassed event contracts one day in September, but on Friday perps topped prediction markets volume for a second day. Now Kalshi expects that performance to continue as it introduces perps tied to more individual stocks. On Monday, for example, Kalshi launched contracts linked to Anthropic.

Kalshi was the first to debut perps in the U.S. after winning federal regulatory approval in May to list perps tied to cryptocurrencies.

Perps trading volume includes any leverage that speculators acquire along with their trade, while event contracts are fully collateralized — for now.

Since the original launch in May, Kalshi has received approval to introduce perps tied to metals, crude oil, stock indexes and individual stocks.

Offshore perps — those available on exchanges not regulated in the U.S. — generated more than $90 trillion in notional trading volume in 2025, so it's not surprising that the product has grown so rapidly on Kalshi, according to Udesh Jha, chief risk officer at Kalshi Klear, the company's clearing house.

"We're just in very early innings. We're launching products, we're growing the participant base."

Perps were Kalshi's first product to mark its transition from a prediction market-focused platform to a full-blown financial exchange where various assets are traded. Last week, reports said that Kalshi is planning to offer trading on equities on its platform in the coming months.

At the same time, the company's perps product has come under fire. Some incumbent exchanges where futures are traded — which saw their stock prices decline following the approval of U.S. perps — believe the product was improperly approved. CME Group is suing the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal derivatives regulator, for approving perps.

Others have simply expressed concerns about the efficiency of the markets. CNBC previously reported that trading volume on Kalshi's most popular perps markets — tied to bitcoin and ether cryptocurrencies — was dramatically greater than open interest, or cash actively in the markets. It's a phenomenon that isn't common with U.S.-regulated traditional futures, nor other offshore perps markets.

Kalshi said at the time it has "zero concerns" about the distinction, and that it appears because less leverage is offered compared to offshore exchanges and there are fewer incentives for traders to park capital on its perps markets.

While Kalshi started with cryptocurrencies, Owen Lau, an analyst at Clear Street, said perps tied to individual stocks likely represent the most promising opportunity for growth in the U.S.

"That's how I foresee the way perps will penetrate further into traditional asset classes," Lau said. "Perps on single stocks and [key performance indicators on individual companies] could change how investors hedge their portfolio or even make a directional bet."

Kalshi's growth has been powered by the fact that right now it's the only exchange that can actively list perps in the U.S., though crypto exchange Coinbase received approval in May to route U.S. users to offshore platforms for trading. That monopoly status, however, will probably prove short lived.

Coinbase has filed to list single-stock perps in the U.S., and President Donald Trump in August said the CFTC is working to bring Hyperliquid — a dominant player in offshore perps activity — to domestic traders.

But Jha at Kalshi isn't worried about the competition.

"What will carry us is ... making sure that we have the right products for the marketplace, making sure we have the right surveillance of the products that we are trading."

Disclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

#2701. AI debt markets shudder as Nvidia's top 'banker' returns

AI credit markets are shuddering again with Jensen Huang back as CEO of Nvidia.

Fears about the massive debt being taken on to fund the artificial intelligence buildout climbed Tuesday as Wall Street weighed what Huang's return to Nvidia means for its bankrolling of the AI boom.

Huang is considered one of the top financiers, or bankers, in the AI industry, spearheading deals with neoclouds like CoreWeave and other firms to buy chips, backed in some cases by Nvidia guarantees. His return to Nvidia has revived prospects for the company to continue "circular financing" of AI chips and data centers — raising concerns among credit investors.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child of AI debt concerns, saw its stock sink 13% and the yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 top 17%. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

At the same time, the spread on the neocloud company's five-year credit default swaps jumped 8.5% to over 1,200 basis points. Credit default swaps are insurance against nonpayment and are considered a barometer of perceived risks. Rising CDS spreads mean investors view the debt as riskier.

Huang was reinstated as CEO on Monday after stepping down on Nov. 12 amid allegations of multiple affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy. His reinstatement on Monday was cheered by investors, who pushed stocks higher, yields lower and spreads on CDS tighter. However, stocks retreated, bond yields rose and CDS spreads widened on Tuesday.

Ben Emons, founder and chief investment officer at FedWatch Advisors, called it a waning of the "Jensen effect."

The moves suggest "markets see government intervention as 'moral suasion' that carries credit and interest-rate risks," he said.

President Donald Trump told CNBC on Monday he "convinced" the board to bring Huang back.

CoreWeave wasn't the only name seeing heightened concerns in CDS spreads. Oracle's five-year CDS spread jumped 7% to 355.68. Even highly rated hyperscalers Meta Platforms and Amazon.com saw spreads widen by more than 2%. Nvidia's CDS added 3.4%.

Larry Holzenthaler, senior portfolio manager for fixed income at Catalyst Funds, believes the drama that unfolded with Huang's return to Nvidia won't necessarily sit well with credit investors.

"A lot of old school credit people are going to look at what kind of materialized there, the administration's involvement in putting him back in, and I think a lot of credit participants are going to step back and tiptoe away from that a bit," he said. "Credit market investors typically don't like that type of drama or uncertainty."

While Nvidia has commitments across the AI ecosystem, it is the neoclouds that have been under the most scrutiny. Many of the companies, which rent out AI computing power and cloud capacity, are highly leveraged and have relied on Nvidia financing to reduce their exposure to the bond market.

With so much riding on Nvidia's funding, Huang's next move is being closely watched.

During his brief absence, chief financial officer Colette Kress said during the company's earnings call that Nvidia would be "rigorously evaluating future investments" and will remain disciplined in how it commits capital.

That suggested Nvidia was going to be more judicious with financing, says Paul Meeks, head of technology research at Freedom Capital Markets.

"That concern should be put to rest with Jensen [Huang] back," he said.

Investor Steve Eisman, of "Big Short" fame and host of "The Real Eisman Playbook" podcast, believes Huang feels emboldened now that he's back in charge.

"[H]e'll double down on the circular financing," Eisman predicted on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Tuesday.

After Huang's departure, Eisman believed that the ecosystem the CEO created by pouring money into AI companies would likely unwind and leave some of the companies in "big trouble."

"Now that he's back, they're not," he said.

Others are not so certain the level of funding will continue.

"Given scrutiny of disclosure around financing and guarantees … we do not expect Mr. Huang's return to bring a quick reversion to broader customer financing," Stifel analyst Ruben Roy said in a note Monday.

Nvidia said on its earnings call that it has $118 billion in guarantees, as of Oct. 25, to back AI projects.

Concerns about the level of debt to fund the AI infrastructure buildout had already taken hold before Huang's departure and reinstatement.

"These issues have not disappeared just because the White House pressured the weak board to reinstate Jensen Huang," said economist David Rosenberg, founder and president of Rosenberg Research.

John Lloyd, global head of multi-sector and corporate credit at Janus Henderson Investors, believes having Huang back at the helm "reaffirms his existing go-to-market strategy." However, the credit market is still taking a cautious look at the neoclouds as it waits for more clarity on long-term supply/demand dynamics.

Still, Lloyd is cautiously positive on CoreWeave, which he owns in portfolios he manages, and noted all the data point to a "pretty healthy environment right now." That includes strong residual values on graphics processing units and spot compute rates, he noted.

"The company is doing everything in its power to execute," he said. "They don't need the high yield market at this time."

In the meantime, investigations into Nvidia and Huang are ramping up. Huang is expected to appear before three House committees next week. Nvidia is conducting an independent investigation into his activities, and California Attorney General Rob Bonta has launched a probe. At the federal level, President Trump said Monday that U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche "has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct."

"There's other shoes to drop," Rosenberg said. "I don't think that the book has been closed on this file."

#2700. NBA champ blasts Luka Doncic, Lakers ahead of clash with Spurs for best in West

The Lakers' early-season schedule has been a point of contention, but the team's biggest test of the season is on Friday when Los Angeles takes on the Spurs.

San Antonio earned its 15th win of the season Monday, as did the Lakers. The two West rivals boast the best record in the conference, but Spurs color commentator Sean Elliott isn't convinced by Los Angeles' strong start to the campaign.

Jacob Tobey and Sean Elliott smiles during the game between the Utah Jazz and San Antonio Spurs at the Frost Bank Center in San Antonio, Texas on October 9, 2024. NBAE via Getty Images

"Well, the Lakers aren't gonna win the NBA championship. They're not," Elliott said bluntly on the game broadcast Monday as San Antonio defeated the Kings.

"I mean, they'll be fun to watch. They have really good players. I like Mamu in a Laker uniform. Plus, your best player always, he's gotta be a stalwart on the defensive end of the floor. I firmly believe that."

Elliott, a former NBA champion with the Spurs in 1999, built a reputation for being a solid two-way player during his career, particularly on the defensive end of the floor. Clearly, he is not a believer that Doncic has made many strides in that area, despite what many people say.

He went on to list the Spurs, Thunder, Knicks and 76ers as potential championship teams. In spite of the mass amount of injuries for Oklahoma City, the former NBA champion believes they have a better chance at this year's title than the Lakers do.

Luka Doncic #77 of the Los Angeles Lakers looks on during the game against the Utah Jazz on November 23, 2026 at Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, California. NBAE via Getty Images

San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama walks up court between plays in the second half of an NBA basketball game against the New Orleans Pelicans, Saturday, Nov. 21, 2026, in San Antonio. AP Photo/Darren Abate

The heavy usage of Luka Doncic has also been a sticking point for skeptics. Doncic is central to helping the Lakers make a deep playoff run, but many argue his workload is unsustainable throughout the regular season and beyond.

Earlier on the broadcast, Elliott praised Doncic for his otherworldly performance this season, but noted that his usage rate quickly puts the purple and gold out of championship contention.

He is averaging just over 36 minutes per game. But that is nothing new for the Slovenian sharpshooter. Doncic has averaged between 32 and 37 minutes every season of his nine-year career.

Nevertheless, Friday's game should be a fair litmus test for the Lakers and their skeptics.

#2699. Bears Have Plenty to Be Thankful For, But Lions Won’t Be Very Giving

Thanksgiving is supposed to be a time to appreciate what you have. For the Chicago Bears, there is plenty worth celebrating.

An 8-2 record, five consecutive victories, and a defense transformed by the arrival of Jeffery Simmons have Chicago looking like a legitimate NFC contender. Sunday's 21-13 victory over the New Orleans Saints offered another reminder of how far this team has come under head coach Ben Johnson.

However, Thanksgiving dinner comes with a warning this year. The Detroit Lions are also 8-2, riding a six-game winning streak and preparing to welcome a division rival to Ford Field.

Chicago has found ways to win when its offense hasn't been at its best. Against Detroit, finding a way will not be easy.

Sunday's victory over New Orleans was another demonstration of what Chicago's defense has become since acquiring Simmons from the Tennessee Titans.

The Bears recorded six sacks, forced two turnovers, and produced a safety against rookie quarterback Tyler Shough. Simmons accounted for three sacks, matching his career high, while Montez Sweat added a safety that helped preserve Chicago's advantage in the fourth quarter.

The impact extended beyond the stat sheet. In the second quarter, Clark Phillips III forced a fumble that Austin Booker recovered, giving Chicago possession at the New Orleans 41-yard line. Caleb Williams capitalized with a three-yard touchdown pass to D'Andre Swift. On the Saints' following possession, rookie safety Dillon Thieneman intercepted Shough after pressure from Sweat. Williams responded by finding Colston Loveland for a 15-yard touchdown, highlighted by the rookie tight end hurdling safety Julian Blackmon on his way into the end zone.

Those two takeaways helped Chicago establish a 16-0 lead before New Orleans could respond. They also showed how effectively the Bears' defense can create scoring opportunities for an offense that has occasionally struggled to manufacture them on its own.

"I couldn't be more proud of our defensive effort here today," Johnson said after the win, praising the unit's ability to generate sacks and turn turnovers into offensive opportunities.

Simmons has recorded five sacks in three games since arriving in Chicago. His presence has given the Bears another disruptive force alongside Sweat, making their defensive front increasingly difficult to handle. The question heading into Thanksgiving is whether that pressure can remain as effective against a Detroit offense built to punish defensive mistakes.

For all the positives surrounding Chicago's defense, Sunday's offensive performance raised concerns.

Williams completed 15 of 23 passes for 181 yards, two touchdowns and an interception. While his two scoring passes helped establish an early lead, the Bears struggled to turn their remaining possessions into touchdowns. Chicago finished with 311 net yards, and its offense managed just five points after halftime, both coming from Cairo Santos field goals before Sweat's safety accounted for the final two points.

The interception was not simply a case of Williams making an inaccurate throw. New Orleans defensive lineman Khristian Boyd deflected a pass intended for Luther Burden III, allowing linebacker Danny Stutsman to secure the interception. The play demonstrated how a disrupted passing lane can turn an otherwise routine attempt into a costly turnover.

Chicago's other giveaway was more damaging in terms of field position and timing. After Sweat's safety extended the lead to 21-10, the Bears got the ball near midfield. On the first play, Saints defensive end Carl Granderson stripped Swift, and Julian Blackmon recovered the football. Instead of potentially putting the game away, Chicago handed New Orleans another opportunity to make it a one-possession contest.

Williams acknowledged afterward that the offense had missed opportunities. "I think there was opportunity for a lot of points out there, whether it's us being on the same page, us being efficient running and efficient passing," Williams said.

That assessment matters heading into Detroit. The Lions have demonstrated an ability to score quickly, and Chicago cannot assume its defense will repeatedly provide a favorable field position. Williams does not need to produce a flawless performance on Thanksgiving. However, protecting the football, sustaining drives, and capitalizing on scoring opportunities will be essential if the Bears intend to keep pace with Detroit.

While Chicago relied heavily on its defense Sunday, Detroit demonstrated why its offense remains one of the NFC's most dangerous units.

The Lions defeated the Tampa Bay Buccaneers 31-21 behind another efficient performance from Jared Goff. The veteran quarterback completed 20 of 28 passes for 279 yards, two touchdowns and no interceptions. His touchdown passes highlighted Detroit's ability to attack defenses in different ways. Goff connected with Amon-Ra St. Brown for a 14-yard score before finding Jameson Williams for a 57-yard touchdown.

That combination creates a difficult assignment for Chicago's secondary. St. Brown can consistently threaten underneath and intermediate coverage, while Williams' speed forces defenses to account for explosive plays downfield.

Detroit also possesses a difference-maker in the backfield. Jahmyr Gibbs scored twice in the fourth quarter against Tampa Bay, helping the Lions turn a competitive game into a double-digit victory. His ability to contribute as both a runner and receiver makes him particularly dangerous against defenses that commit too many resources to stopping the passing game.

For Chicago, that creates a balancing act. Simmons and Sweat must generate pressure without allowing Goff to exploit openings created by an aggressive pass rush. Meanwhile, the Bears' linebackers and defensive backs must remain disciplined against Gibbs and Detroit's receiving weapons.

The Lions converted seven of their 11 third-down opportunities against Tampa Bay, an efficiency rate of 63.6%. That ability to extend possessions could limit Chicago's opportunities to control the game through defensive pressure and takeaways.

The Bears have built an identity around making opponents uncomfortable. Detroit has the personnel to make Chicago uncomfortable in return.

Thanksgiving also brings another chapter in one of the NFL's most compelling coaching storylines.

Johnson returns to Ford Field as Chicago's head coach after previously serving as Detroit's offensive coordinator. His arrival helped reshape the Bears' offensive identity and contributed to Chicago winning the NFC North in his first season.

However, the Lions swept both meetings with Chicago last season, demonstrating that Johnson's familiarity with Detroit did not automatically translate into success against his former team.

There is also history attached to this particular holiday matchup. On Thanksgiving in 2024, Chicago suffered a 23-20 loss to Detroit after a disastrous final possession in which the Bears failed to manage the remaining time properly. Head coach Matt Eberflus was fired the following day, setting in motion the changes that eventually brought Johnson to Chicago.

Two years later, the circumstances are dramatically different. Rather than entering Ford Field searching for answers, the Bears arrive as a division contender with an opportunity to strengthen their position in the NFC North. Detroit, however, has its own reasons to approach the matchup with confidence.

Despite playing without injured defensive star Aidan Hutchinson, the Lions recorded four sacks against Tampa Bay. Their defense also limited the Buccaneers to 274 total yards, showing that Detroit's success doesn't depend exclusively on its offense.

That makes Thursday a significant examination of Johnson's Bears. Chicago must find ways to move the football against a defense capable of creating pressure while also containing one of the league's more explosive offenses.

The Bears have earned the right to feel confident entering Thanksgiving.

Five consecutive victories do not happen by accident. Chicago has developed a defense capable of changing games, a young quarterback who continues to grow, and a coaching staff that has established a winning culture.

But Detroit has been equally impressive, winning six straight games and demonstrating the ability to close out opponents on both sides of the ball.

Thursday's matchup will not decide the entire NFC North race, but it will provide an important indication of where both teams stand entering the final stretch of the regular season.

For Chicago, the formula cannot simply be to wait for Simmons or Sweat to deliver another game-changing play. Williams and the offense must contribute consistently enough to prevent Detroit from dictating the pace. The Bears have plenty to be thankful for this season. A winning record, renewed expectations, and meaningful Thanksgiving football are all signs of progress.

But if Chicago wants to leave Ford Field with another reason to celebrate, they will have to earn every bit of it.

The Lions won't be giving away anything for free.

#2695. Fantasy Football Rankings: Hayden Winks' WR Blueprint for Week 12

The Blueprint is my weekly column and basically everything that I use to build out the most accurate rankings I can. There will be an RB column, this WR column and a combination column on the onesie positions. You will find film notes and endless charts. Maybe enough charts to stress test the Yahoo website. I kid.

It's impossible to get every ranking thoroughly early in the week, so be sure to keep checking in on these columns through Sunday morning. As always, my full rankings at every position will be updated here soon.

1. Ja'Marr Chase (vs. NO) - 93.5 proj. receiving yards

2. Jaxon Smith-Njigba (at SF) - 97.5 proj. receiving yards

Smith-Njigba is the WR2 in per-game half PPR scoring on WR6 expected-points usage over his past four games with Drew Lock and Sam Darnold splitting time. He has topped 100 receiving yards in three of those four contests while drawing a 44% target share in that span. What's new?

San Francisco ranks 11th in half PPR points allowed per game to opposing wideouts, having surrendered 71.2 fantasy points to the Cowboys receiver room in Week 10 when chasing points. JSN has tons of experience against this defense, most recently posting 118, 19, 84, 124 and 118 yards. Seattle travels as 3-point road underdogs with a 21.75-point team total (17th). Throwing the ball to the perimeter is the best way to move the ball against the Niners, in my opinion.

3. CeeDee Lamb (vs. PHI) - 89.5 proj. receiving yards

Lamb is the WR3 on WR2 usage this year, ranking second in targets per game (11.8) and third in yards per game (100.7). Through 11 weeks of an NFL season, Lamb's 208.2 half PPR points are 13th all-time. All-time.

The Eagles have been bad against Lamb-type receivers all year and now won't have All Pro LB Zack Baun. They've allowed the third-most points to fantasy WRs, and Lamb finished as the WR5 on WR1 overall usage against them in Week 7. Dallas carries a 28-point team total (fourth) as 8.5-point home favorites.

4. Amon-Ra St. Brown (vs. CHI) - 84.5 proj. receiving yards

St. Brown is having his usual season. He's the WR5 on WR7 usage, after going on a touchdown-less rut throughout October.

This matchup has the potential for a blowup game. The biggest factor will be if slot CB Kyler Gordon can play after he missed last week. The Bears have been pretty woeful in the secondary beyond him, while shutting down the run since Jeffery Simmons appeared. The Sun God was the WR5 and WR1 in matchups against them last year, both wins for Detroit. Jaxon Smith-Njigba hung 118-1 against them in Week 8 in a similar role, too. Detroit enters as 2.5-point home underdogs carrying a 26.5-point implied team total (sixth).

5. Tee Higgins (vs. NO) - 70.5 proj. receiving yards

6. Parker Washington (vs. TEN) - 78.5 proj. receiving yards

That really should've been a touchdown. Come on, refs! Washington still was a top-20 WR last week and is now the WR13 on WR12 usage across the season. He can be up-and-down based on the Jaguars' lopsided history, but when games are tighter, Washington catches fire, as he did last week when he racked up 16 targets while trailing.

This week, the Jaguars are expected to go crazy on offense. They have a league-high 31.0-point team total against the Titans, who have allowed 362 passing yards per game over the past month. Read that again. And again. It's one of the wildest stats of the year. It doesn't take a genius to feel good about Washington's ceiling odds here. He had 152-1 against them just two weeks ago.

7. George Pickens (vs. PHI) - 70.5 proj. receiving yards

We're so back. Pickens has 38.0 and 20.3 half PPR points, respectively, in his two games since the bye. He had one of the best grabs of the year last week along the sideline, while Dak Prescott had all day to pass behind a great Cowboys OL. It's an environment for Pickens to have monster games, even if his role and style come with some volatility. He's at his best when teams go to single high coverage, something the Eagles typically don't do.

That said, CB1 Quinyon Mitchell is dealing with a new hamstring injury, and the other star players won't be available with Jordan Davis on the Jaguars and LB Zack Baun on IR. Mitchell's status is a big deal for Pickens' matchup. Across the season, the Eagles have had far too many blown coverages, leading to the third-most fantasy points allowed to WRs (31.3). Pickens had 57-1 against them in Week 7 and 146-1 against them late last year. Dallas carries a 28-point team total (fourth) as 8.5-point home favorites.

8. Malik Nabers (at IND) - 64.5 proj. receiving yards

Nabers had a handful of underneath receptions against elite CB1 Travis Hunter last week, then teleported into the back of the end zone against Jacksonville's nickel defender to bring Nabers to a top-15 WR finish. Since Week 4, Nabers is the WR9 on WR4 usage with Puka Nacua as one of the receivers ahead. Things will always be up-and-down with J.J. McCarthy, who missed him way out of bounds for a potential back-shoulder TD, but Nabers is way too good to not be treated as a fantasy WR1 now.

The Giants have a healthy 24.0-point team total this week, and that'll easily be one of their best all year. The Colts are tanking and have allowed the 10th-most passing yards per game over their last four games. We'll see if CB1 Sauce Gardner or CB2 Charvarius Ward will return this week. Nico Collins had an awesome deep touchdown against their backups last week, and Nabers had a 171-2 game against the Colts during his rookie season, for what it's worth. Long story short, Nabers looks great this week.

9. Justin Jefferson (vs. ATL) - 84.5 proj. receiving yards

Jefferson is the WR18 on WR8 usage over the past two weeks with Kirk Cousins. The fumble on that in-cut explosion was a real bummer, but that completion had a lot of timing and anticipation from the QB, something Jefferson hasn't had since 2023. He had plenty of breaking routes against the 49ers, and Kevin O'Connell drew up two different downfield shots to him, too. A big game is long overdue. The signs of it happening soon are there.

This is a sweet matchup for just that. The Falcons don't have Pro Bowl FS Jessie Bates, and CB1 A.J. Terrell is having a down season in isolation. The Vikings getting their OL healthy again would be nice, but Jefferson should have room to operate either way. The Falcons have allowed the fifth-most passing yards per game this year and the seventh-most fantasy points to WRs. Minnesota has a strong 24.75-point team total, and Jordan Addison (finger) isn't expected to play.

10. Nico Collins (vs. BAL) - 63.5 proj. receiving yards

Collins ranks as the WR18 in half PPR points per game on WR31 expected-points usage across his last four appearances. His weekly target volume has fluctuated wildly, bottoming out at four targets in two separate contests while spiking to 15 targets in Week 10 against Cleveland. The good news is the Texans have recently ramped his snap rates up out of desperation and with Marvin Harrison Jr. and Jaylen Noel sidelined. Collins is the WR11 on WR20 usage this year. That's a fair range for him. A long dunk-on-you TD made him the WR18 last week.

Baltimore's defense has underwhelmed. We'll see if podcaster Marlon Humphrey is back this week, but he's been bad this year anyway. Collins will likely see a bunch of CB1 Nate Wiggins, who has the speed to match with Collins downfield. Opponents facing the Ravens have posted a 46% neutral pass rate, the third-lowest rate in the NFL and the Texans are 6.5-point home favorites. He likely won't have that many targets here, but a 26.5-point team total (seventh) suggests he'll be a big reason why that is.

11. Matthew Golden (at LAR) - 74.5 proj. receiving yards

Golden has produced as the WR8 in half PPR points per game on WR5 expected-points usage over his last four games. The breakout sophomore has commanded a 33% target share alongside 10.8 targets and 133 air yards per game, topping nine targets in all four contests. These are the type of metrics that make the drops livable. Golden is one of the best separators in the NFL. Full stop.

The Rams present a stingy draw on paper, ranking 30th in half PPR points allowed to WRs (21.5 per game). Opposing offenses have largely avoided testing them through the air, but have CB2 Jaylen Watson on IR right now, at least. Golden may see a handful of Trent McDuffie in this one, so he may not be as open as he usually is. The Packers simply don't have other avenues to move the ball, so Golden should still see plenty of looks. Green Bay is listed as 3-point road underdogs with a 20.75-point team total (19th).

12. Christian Watson (at LAR) - 75.5 proj. receiving yards

Watson is the WR7 on WR16 usage this season, while the past month has cooled off (WR15 on WR28 usage). He's already faced the Vikings twice and the Bucs this year, and he's been masterful in the other contests. Green Bay won't have Josh Jacobs and will need its signature splash plays to win on Thanksgiving Eve on the road.

The Rams have been tough on WRs, ranking 30th in half PPR points allowed to the position at 21.5 per game. They also sit 27th against deep passes over 15 air yards, allowing only 6.3 points per game on downfield attempts. Their structure is to stop this aerial offense, but easier said than done. CB2 Jaylen Watson being on IR certainly helps Watson's odds. Green Bay travels as 3-point road underdogs with an implied team total of 20.75 points (19th).

13. Mike Evans (vs. SEA) - 59.5 proj. receiving yards

Removing screens, Evans is the WR1 overall in yards per route (4.1) this season as a 33-year-old grown man. He's been a total monster at the catch point as usual, and the 49ers are often in the red zone to take advantage of his size and ball tracking. He's the WR12 on WR19 usage throughout the year, including his injured games. He put up 109 yards against the dang Vikings in Mexico City last week and his best game of the year was against the Seahawks. He doesn't care about matchups.

Speaking of, it's rematch SZN with Evans taking on Seattle at home here. He dunked all over CB2 Josh Jobe in Week 5, when he was the WR6 on WR5 usage. That's largely been the only great game at receiver against the Seahawks all year, with nobody posting more than 60 yards at WR since. He's been the WR25 on WR17 usage this year, through no fault of his own. He's the WR3 overall in ESPN's on-field tracking metrics, and I've seen him wide open way too often on inaccurate passes. He's turned 12.8 expected points per game into 8.1 points this month. That does make him a positive regression candidate, though we've said that for his entire career.
